response.translation: But the disease that does pass through them all is disputed with regard to practically every one of its parts. Some say that the peak is a single moment of time [441], grasped by conception alone; others, that in the continuous fevers (synochoi) there is no peak at all; others introduce the peak into a beginning of short duration; others take away the beginning, not only in these but in all the remaining diseases as well; and others sometimes take away the decline too, if the disease is resolved by 'abscission' (ex apokopēs), as they call it. First, then, these disputes must be settled; then the notions of the periods of the whole disease must be precisely articulated; after that their signs must be stated; and next it would remain to show their usefulness, combining it with what concerns the cycles. Now the beginning of the disease, insofar as it sets in at some moment when the healthy state collapses, is conceived in all of them without any extension of time. response.translation: For, falling away [442] from the natural state, they have their coming-into-being in an instant of time, and from there they ascend up to the peak. For let the disease be, say, one consisting in a dyscrasia, the condition in which we have shown fever too to be constituted. It is necessary, then, that as soon as this unnatural heat first arises, the person is feverish, and that the heat is intensified up to the peak. 'For of that which has no parts, how could there be a coming-into-being in time?' These things were said by me right at the beginning as well, and I answered them by recalling the fevers that set in with chilling. But in the case of the periods the answer is sufficient; for the time of the chilling is one of the partial times of the whole disease, and the first in order. It would, however, be most ridiculous to regard the first time of the first paroxysm as the beginning of the whole disease. For this time, which they call the beginning of a disease, has its usefulness with respect to the remedies, and it was looking to this that he said: 'When diseases are beginning, if anything seems to need moving, move it; but when they are at their peak, it is better to keep quiet.'

raw_text: {"translation": "When it is now changing into pus, then, I suppose, the greatest pains [445] take hold. For pains and fevers occur around the generation of pus rather than once it has been generated; and such a period is called the acme of the affection. But if the flux, by suppurating or by being dispersed, renders both the swelling and the tension smaller, this is the beginning of the decline. In this way, then, the periods are distinguished in the case of inflammation. In the case of fever, for a fever that arises upon an inflammation one is to posit the same periods as for the inflammation. For one that arises upon a humour without inflammation, the time of the lack of concoction of the troublesome humours is to be posited as the beginning. When they begin to be concocted, the beginning has ended and the second period has arrived, the one named that of the ascent. When the concoction itself is most fully being accomplished, that is the period of the acme. Then next comes that of the decline, in which both the magnitude of the symptoms and the quantity of the matters being concocted have already ceased, and there is still a small remnant of the humours that need to be concocted.", "renderings": [{"target_no": 19, "surface": "πύου", "english": "pus", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 52, "surface": "παρακμῆς", "english": "decline", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 87, "surface": "ἀπεψίας", "english": "lack of concoction", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 108, "surface": "ἀναβάσεως", "english": "ascent", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 144, "surface": "λείψανον", "english": "remnant", "uncertain": "n"}], "uncertain_greek": ["γενέσιας", "ἐκπυϊσκόμενον", "πεπαῦσθαι"]}

I went through these at very great length in that discussion, together with the Hippocratic passages; on the present occasion it is enough to say only this much: ulcers too have the same periods. For first watery, unconcocted and thin ichors flow from them; then next, ichors that are fewer and thicker; and after that, by now, thin pus; then this becomes less in quantity, but thicker and whiter. response.translation: And who, having seen thin sputum coughed up in pleuritis or peripneumonia, will not likewise understand that it is still [447] the beginning of the affection? So too in ophthalmias: at the beginning there flows off much thin matter, quite unconcocted; next, less and thicker, taking on some trace of concoction; then, as time goes on, with the quantity diminishing and the consistency tending towards the thicker, the signs of concoction increase to such a degree that the eyelids of those who have slept are even glued together by the rheum that has formed. This rheum, too, is thin and abundant at the start, but with time becomes less and thicker, and so indicates both the concoction of the disease and its decline. Moreover, in the case of what flows down from the brain through the palate and the nostrils, it is the beginning when what is carried down is watery and thin and abundant and acrid, for these things indicate extreme non-concoction. The distinguishing marks of concoction, by now, are that the discharge is thicker and less acrid and is evacuated in small quantity. If what is called mucus and slime should also come away with it, this is already a surer sign of concoction; just as, indeed, (if) it becomes thicker and less abundant, it indicates concoction much more still. raw_text: {"translation": "And [the disease is] great also if, in pleuritics and peripneumonics, the sputum is either black, or intensely tawny, or frothy, or considerably foul-smelling, or is not brought up at all, while violent pain or dyspnoea [458] grips the patient. Hence it is not possible to define the acme in such diseases in the same way as the acme of those who are going to be saved. For there the greatest paroxysms marked off the acme, but here one cannot define the greatest ones in the same way, since the disease is not being concocted at all. Rather, one must grasp by conception the greatest [extent], which the disease sometimes reaches, while at other times it kills [the patient] before reaching it.
